text: Rated Low because there is no data behind the portal to process at all - the "effort" is simply browsing a website, not because the source is easy to make portfolio-ready (see key_limitation).
Good as entry point/screening level, too coarse for populating data points.
NUTS-aggregated layers usable directly; finer layers (SHP/raster) require geocoding and spatial overlay.
Well suited to substantive risk determination (col. 0050); over-specified for the pure Geography reporting requirement.

Rated High: the raw fire danger index (GeoTIFF, varies daily) and historical burnt-area layer have no ready-made exposure score, unlike the Low-rated BWV/HQ30 and WLV vector datasets - both require own geocoding, index interpretation and GIS overlay.
Free, CC-BY 4.0 (attribution only).
Raw climate variables (NetCDF grid data) without ready-made risk classification; requires climatological/GIS processing.
Since 2 July 2025 uniformly CC-BY 4.0; individual sub-datasets may carry stricter licences (e.g. E-OBS: non-commercial research/education only) - verify per dataset.
Not suitable for populating individual exposures; useful for benchmarking/peer comparison only.
Traceable methodology replicable with AnaCredit/JRC/Copernicus; useful methodological anchor, operates at NUTS3 rather than country level.

Single national dataset (HQ30/HQ100/HQ300 flood extent family) with its own INSPIRE Atom download service and WMS/WFS endpoints; requires geocoding of portfolio locations and a standard spatial overlay, but no merging of separate state datasets - the same pipeline shape as the WLV Gefahrenzonenplan.

Covers riverine flood hazard (BWV) with the same subject-matter content as HORA but usable without legal restriction. Scope narrowed to flood: torrent, avalanche and mass-movement hazards are covered nationally and more consistently by the WLV Gefahrenzonenplan.

Rated Low (revised from an earlier Medium rating): a single national shapefile dataset with its own download service; requires geocoding and a standard spatial overlay, but no merging of separate state datasets - consistent with bundeslaender_open_data (BWV/HQ30), which has near-identical technical characteristics.

The strongest national source for mass-movement and torrent hazards: a statutory hazard assessment under the Forstgesetz covering torrents, avalanches and erosion processes (rockfall, landslide, debris flow), published as a High Value Dataset. Complements rather than duplicates the BWV flood data, which covers riverine flooding.
High Value Dataset under Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/138; free of charge, bulk download via the WLV download service, ESRI shapefile format.

Design event is an approximately 150-year return period. Zones are process boundaries rather than inundation lines and include erosion processes and sediment transport, so they are not directly comparable to the BWV flood inundation areas.
Suitable for individual address-level checks only, not for systematic portfolio classification.
Free for individual queries; separate agreement with operator (LFRZ) required for portfolio-level use.
Good supplementary dataset for chronic risk (water stress), since AT sources primarily cover acute hazards.
Ready-made risk scores per location, directly integrable via API.
High data quality and granularity; cost structure typically not designed for SNCI scale.
Ready-made scores/maps via web tool or API.
Very extensive (scenarios to 2100); commercial, geared towards larger institutions/reinsurers.
Country-level granularity too coarse for exposure/NUTS assignment; useful for plausibility checks only.
Best available current Austrian permafrost source for context/discussion; not suitable for exposure-level classification.

Single CSV file (326,479 records) keyed to the Firmenbuch number; joins directly to a loan portfolio without GIS or geocoding work. Codes are 5-digit OeNACE; the 4-digit NACE level required by D 01.01 is obtained by dropping the last digit.

The strongest transition-risk source identified: official assignment under section 21 Bundesstatistikgesetz, published as a High Value Dataset under CC BY 4.0, covering all actively registered Austrian companies with an assigned economic activity. Resolves the previous trade-off in which official quality and open access were mutually exclusive.
CC BY 4.0, published under Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/138 (High Value Datasets); free of charge, bulk download, updated continuously.

Verified as OeNACE 2025 / NACE Rev. 2.1 by structural analysis of the 682 distinct codes: division 45 absent (abolished in Rev. 2.1), classes 47.41/47.42/47.43 absent (merged into 47.40), class 46.89 present (newly created in Rev. 2.1), and divisions 62 and 63 following the Rev. 2.1 structure. Template D 01.01 uses the same revision, as evidenced by its designation K.63 for computing infrastructure, which is only valid under Rev. 2.1. No transcoding between classification versions is therefore required.
Ready-made OeNACE 2025 classification per entity, delivered via API; no manual extract handling required.

Retained alongside the HVD dataset because access already exists institutionally in parts of the Austrian banking sector (for example across the Raiffeisen sector), making the marginal cost zero and an existing query operationally simpler than downloading and joining the HVD file. Adds daily currency and coverage beyond the Firmenbuch.

technical_effort reflects the effort to access and use the source's own data (dashboard-only, no download/API, same interface as EBA ESG Dashboard, hence Low). The separate, substantially higher effort of replicating the ECB's methodology with AnaCredit/JRC/Copernicus-equivalent inputs is a distinct undertaking and is described in the abstract, not folded into this column.
Not applicable - see key_limitation.

(1) Geocode exposure addresses to coordinates. (2) Identify the NUTS2/3 region for each coordinate. (3) Download/query the relevant hazard module(s) via API or shapefile. (4) Join exposures to their region's value. Regional (not parcel-level) result.

(1) Geocode exposure addresses to coordinates. (2) Query the WMS/WFS or download the GeoTIFF fire danger index / burnt-area layer. (3) Extract the raster cell value at each coordinate (point-in-raster lookup). (4) Decide how to handle the time-varying daily index (e.g. seasonal maximum or long-run average) to arrive at a single static attribute per exposure.

(1) Geocode exposure addresses to coordinates. (2) Select and download the relevant climate variable(s) in NetCDF/GRIB. (3) Derive a hazard-relevant indicator from the raw climate variable (this is a climatological modelling step, not a simple lookup). (4) Extract the grid-cell value at each coordinate.
Not applicable - see key_limitation.

Not applicable via this source directly (see key_limitation). A per-exposure pipeline would instead need to replicate the ECB's published methodology using the bank's own AnaCredit-equivalent data plus JRC/Copernicus hazard layers.

(1) Geocode exposure addresses to coordinates. (2) Query the WFS endpoint (nz-core:HazardArea) with each coordinate, or download the GML/shapefile once and perform a local spatial join. (3) Assign the returned zone/extent value to the exposure. Fully automatable, parcel-level result.

(1) Geocode exposure addresses to coordinates. (2) Query the WMS/WFS endpoint or download the shapefile/GeoPackage once and perform a local spatial join. (3) Assign the returned zone value to the exposure. Fully automatable, parcel-level result within mapped municipalities.
Not applicable at scale - see key_limitation. Practical use is limited to spot-checking individual exposures.

(1) Geocode exposure addresses to coordinates. (2) Download the watershed-level dataset (CSV/GeoPackage) or query the API. (3) Perform a spatial join to the relevant watershed polygon. (4) Assign the watershed's indicator value to the exposure. Automatable, but resolution is watershed- not parcel-level.
Send exposure coordinates/address to the API; receive a facility-level score directly. No further spatial processing required.
Send exposure coordinates/address to the API; receive a facility-level score directly. No further spatial processing required.

(1) Geocode exposure addresses to coordinates. (2) Determine the ADM2 (district) administrative unit for each coordinate. (3) Query the ThinkHazard! API for the hazard level of that district (or download the relevant Risk Data Library dataset for gridded hazards such as landslide and perform a spatial join). (4) Assign the returned district-level value to the exposure. Automatable, but resolution is district- not parcel-level.
Not applicable - see key_limitation.
Bulk-download the CSV and join directly on Firmenbuchnummer against the loan portfolio. No geocoding or spatial processing needed.
Send the Firmenbuchnummer or company identifier to the API; receive the OeNACE classification directly. No further processing required.

Climate-ADAPT is a public knowledge portal operated by the European Environment Agency (EEA) (EEA, n.d.-a). It links to a set of 32 climate hazard indices covering 16 hazard categories, grouped into six IPCC AR6 climatic-impact-driver types (heat and cold, wet and dry, wind, snow and ice, coastal, open ocean) (EEA, 2021). Not all of the matrix's physical hazards are represented: permafrost, landslide and soil erosion have no corresponding index in this set, while heat stress and water stress are only indirectly covered via proxy indices (Universal Thermal Climate Index; aridity) (EEA, 2021). Where covered, the source's own report table resolves only to three European macro-regions (Northern/Central/Southern Europe), placing all of Austria in a single "Central Europe" category with no within-country differentiation at that level, though the underlying interactive European Climate Data Explorer allows finer sub-regional zoom for a subset of the indices (EEA, 2021). The source is accessed through an interactive web map portal and is free to use. In the context of Template D 01.01, it is relevant to data point 0050 as a secondary source. For an SNCI, the source is conditionally suitable because it offers a useful entry point for screening and context, although its coarse, non-spatial resolution makes it unsuitable on its own for classifying individual exposures. In portfolio-readiness terms, the source is not ready: no downloadable or queryable data exists behind the portal, so no automated pipeline can be built against it.

The Risk Data Hub (RDH) is a public multi-hazard risk and loss data platform operated by the Joint Research Centre (JRC) in cooperation with the EU Disaster Risk Management Knowledge Centre (DRMKC) (JRC DRMKC, n.d.). It provides modelled exposure, hazard and historical-event data covering multiple physical hazards at regional (NUTS 2/3) granularity across EU, EFTA and IPA countries (JRC DRMKC, n.d.). The source is accessed through a web map portal, direct download and an API, and is free of charge. In the context of Template D 01.01, it is relevant to data point 0050 as a primary source and secondary to the Geography dimension (0090–0130). For an SNCI, the source is suitable because it combines primary relevance with EU-wide consistent methodology, although its Vulnerability and Risk Analysis modules remain documented by JRC as ongoing work, and finer layers require geocoding and spatial overlay. In portfolio-readiness terms, the source is only partly ready: once geocoded and joined to its NUTS2/3 modules, it differentiates between regions but not between individual exposures within the same region.

EFFIS is a public wildfire information service operated jointly by the JRC and Copernicus Emergency Management Service (JRC/Copernicus EMS, n.d.). It provides daily fire danger indices and historical burnt-area data covering wildfire risk at grid/raster granularity across Europe and the MENA region (JRC/Copernicus EMS, n.d.). The source is accessed through an OGC map service and direct download, and is free of charge under a CC-BY 4.0 licence requiring attribution only. In the context of Template D 01.01, it is relevant to data point 0050 as a secondary source. For an SNCI, the source is conditionally suitable because it is the only dedicated wildfire dataset identified, although the raw hazard-index and event data require own geocoding and GIS overlay before they can support exposure-level classification. In portfolio-readiness terms, the source is only partly ready: once geocoded and queried against its ~1km fire-danger raster, it differentiates across the country but not within a single town or parcel.

The CDS is a public climate data repository operated by ECMWF on behalf of the EU (ECMWF, n.d.). It provides climate variables and derived hazard-relevant reference datasets covering multiple physical hazards at grid/raster granularity globally with an EU focus (ECMWF, n.d.). The source is accessed through a web portal, direct download and an API, and is free of charge, uniformly licensed under CC-BY 4.0 since July 2025 (individual sub-datasets may carry stricter terms). In the context of Template D 01.01, it is relevant to data point 0050 as a primary source and secondary to the Geography dimension. For an SNCI, the source is conditionally suitable because it is authoritative and EU-wide consistent, although the raw NetCDF/GRIB climate variables require climatological and GIS processing before they translate into an exposure classification. In portfolio-readiness terms, the source is not ready for typical Austrian portfolios: its roughly 0.1-0.25 degree grid means most exposures within a regionally concentrated portfolio would share an identical value.

The EBA ESG Dashboard is a public statistics dashboard operated by the European Banking Authority (EBA) (EBA, n.d.-a). It provides aggregated ESG risk indicators at EU bank level, covering both physical and transition risk dimensions at institution/portfolio-level granularity rather than individual exposure level (EBA, n.d.-a). The source is accessed through a web-based statistics dashboard and is free to use. In the context of Template D 01.01, it is relevant only as a benchmarking reference, not to any specific data point. For an SNCI, the source is not suitable for populating individual exposures, although it remains useful for peer-comparison and contextual benchmarking of the institution's own ESG risk profile. This is a technical limitation rather than a granularity one: the output is aggregate bank-level statistics, with no per-exposure data to draw on at all.

This is a public methodological and statistical resource operated by the European Central Bank (ECB) (ECB, n.d.). It provides a documented methodology and euro-area statistics on physical risk exposure, covering physical hazards at institution/portfolio-level granularity (NUTS3-based underlying methodology) (ECB, n.d.). The source is accessed through a statistics dashboard and is free to use, though the underlying data (AnaCredit/RIAD) are not accessible to an SNCI. In the context of Template D 01.01, it is relevant to data points 0050 and 0090–0130 as a secondary source. For an SNCI, the source is conditionally suitable because its documented methodology can be replicated using AnaCredit/JRC/Copernicus-equivalent inputs, although the ECB's own underlying supervisory data are unavailable to a non-significant institution. In portfolio-readiness terms, the source itself is not ready: its output is aggregate/dashboard statistics with no per-exposure data, so any per-exposure use means replicating the methodology with the bank's own data rather than drawing on the ECB source directly.

This is a national flood extent dataset, published via the INSPIRE Geoportal Oesterreich, with the Bundesministerium fuer Land- und Forstwirtschaft, Klima- und Umweltschutz, Regionen und Wasserwirtschaft (BMLUK) as data owner and Umweltbundesamt GmbH as the technical operator (INSPIRE Geoportal Oesterreich, n.d.-b). It combines Abflussuntersuchungen (ABU), HORA data and, in part, the BWV and WLV hazard zoning plans into a single set of flood extent layers for the 30-, 100- and 300-year return periods, covering flood risk at parcel/address-level granularity across Austria (INSPIRE Geoportal Oesterreich, n.d.-b). The source is accessed through OGC WMS/WFS services and direct GML/shapefile download via the INSPIRE Atom download service, and is free of charge under a CC BY 4.0 licence. In the context of Template D 01.01, it is relevant to data point 0050 as a primary source. For an SNCI, the source is suitable because it combines several of the other Austrian hazard sources into ready-made flood extent layers with a standard OGC interface, without HORA's bulk-access restriction. In portfolio-readiness terms, the source is ready: once geocoded, a WFS query or a local spatial join against the downloaded layer assigns a differentiating, parcel-level value to each exposure without further manual adjustment.

The GZP is a public national hazard zoning dataset operated by the Forsttechnischer Dienst fuer Wildbach- und Lawinenverbauung (Federal Ministry BMLUK) (data.gv.at, n.d.-b). It provides a statutory hazard assessment under the Forstgesetz covering torrent, avalanche, landslide and erosion processes at parcel/address-level granularity across Austria (INSPIRE Geoportal Oesterreich, n.d.-a). The source is accessed through an OGC map service and direct download in shapefile/GeoPackage format, and is free of charge as a High Value Dataset under Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/138 (INSPIRE Geoportal Oesterreich, n.d.-a). In the context of Template D 01.01, it is relevant to data point 0050 as a primary source. For an SNCI, the source is suitable because it is the strongest national source for mass-movement and torrent hazards, complementing rather than duplicating the BWV flood data, although hazard zones are mapped only within settled areas of relevance, so an unmatched portfolio location may indicate either no hazard or simply no mapping. In portfolio-readiness terms, the source is ready on the same basis as the BWV flood layers: geocoding plus a WMS/WFS query or local spatial join yields a differentiating, parcel-level value per exposure within mapped municipalities.

HORA (Natural Hazard Overview and Risk Assessment Austria) is a publicly accessible Austrian WebGIS application, operated by the Land-, Forst- und Wasserwirtschaftliche Rechenzentrum (LFRZ) on behalf of the responsible federal ministry (LFRZ, n.d.). It provides address- and cadastral-level initial information on natural hazards, currently covering flood, earthquake, storm, hail and snow (HORA, n.d.), with further hazards such as landslide added over time through cooperation with GeoSphere Austria (BMLUK, n.d.). Access is provided through an interactive web interface and individual location queries; however, portfolio-level use is constrained by restrictions on bulk access to the underlying data. The source is therefore relevant to D 01.01 data point 0050, but not sufficient on its own to support systematic portfolio classification. Within the ESG Data Source Matrix, HORA is classified as a conditionally suitable source for individual validation and exposure-level plausibility checks. This is a technical, not a granularity, limitation: the underlying zoning is parcel-level and would be portfolio-ready if bulk access were available.

The Aqueduct Water Risk Atlas is a public water-risk dataset operated by the World Resources Institute (WRI) (WRI, n.d.). It provides 13 modelled indicators covering water stress, drought risk and both riverine and coastal flood risk at sub-catchment (watershed) granularity globally (WRI, n.d.-b). The source is accessed through a web map portal, direct download and an API, and is free of charge. In the context of Template D 01.01, it is relevant to data point 0050 as a secondary source. For an SNCI, the source is conditionally suitable because it fills a gap in the domestic data landscape for chronic water-related hazards, although its global watershed-level granularity is coarser than the parcel-level Austrian sources for the acute hazards it also covers. In portfolio-readiness terms, the source is only partly ready: once geocoded and spatially joined to its watershed polygons, it differentiates between regions but not within a single watershed.

This is a commercial dataset operated by Moody's ESG Solutions (Moody's, n.d.). The underlying methodology originates from Four Twenty Seven, Inc., a physical-climate-risk data firm founded in 2012, in which Moody's Corporation acquired a majority stake in July 2019 as a Moody's Investors Service affiliate (Moody's, 2019); the acquisition was reported in Moody's own 2019 Form 10-Q as operating within the MIS reportable segment (Moody's, 2019b). It provides proprietary modelled physical climate risk scores covering six hazards (floods, heat stress, hurricanes and typhoons, sea-level rise, water stress, wildfires) at facility/object-level granularity globally (Moody's, n.d.-b); note that the storm hazard is modelled as tropical cyclones specifically, which has limited relevance to Austria. The source is accessed through a commercial analytics platform and an API, and is paid, subject to a commercial licence agreement. In the context of Template D 01.01, it is relevant to data points 0050 and 0090–0130 as a primary source. For an SNCI, the source is conditionally suitable because it offers ready-made, high-granularity risk scores integrable via API with low processing effort, although its cost structure is typically designed for larger institutions rather than an SNCI's scale. In portfolio-readiness terms, the source is fully ready: the API returns a differentiating, facility-level score directly, with no further spatial processing required.

NATHAN Risk Suite is a commercial dataset operated by Munich Re (Munich Re, n.d.). It provides proprietary modelled natural hazard and climate scenario scores covering multiple hazards at facility/object-level granularity globally, including scenarios extending to 2100 (Munich Re, n.d.). Two access models exist: a subscription-based portfolio platform (Business/Corporate tiers, with API access, quote-based pricing) and a subscription-free, pay-per-location "On-Demand" service priced from EUR 100-160 per location depending on package size (Munich Re, n.d.-c). In the context of Template D 01.01, it is relevant to data points 0050 and 0090–0130 as a primary source. For an SNCI, the source is suitable because of its very extensive scenario depth and ready-made scores; unlike the quote-based subscription tiers geared towards larger institutions and reinsurers, the pay-per-location On-Demand option makes single-location or small-scale spot-checks accessible without a full portfolio subscription, though it is not designed for bulk portfolio processing. In portfolio-readiness terms, the subscription/API tier is fully ready: it returns a differentiating, facility-level score directly, with no further spatial processing required.

This is a public dataset collection operated by the World Bank Group in cooperation with GFDRR (World Bank/GFDRR, n.d.), comprising both the historical-event Risk Data Library and the forward-looking, probabilistic ThinkHazard! hazard tool (GFDRR, n.d.). It provides climate and disaster risk data covering multiple hazards, with ThinkHazard! resolving to district (ADM2) level via a public API and the Risk Data Library varying by dataset (GFDRR, n.d.-b), and a development-country focus overall (World Bank/GFDRR, n.d.). The source is accessed through a generic web portal, direct download and an API, and is free of charge. In the context of Template D 01.01, it is relevant only as a context/validation reference, not to a specific data point. For an SNCI, the source is conditionally suitable as a supplementary plausibility check because its district-level granularity is coarser than the parcel-level Austrian sources for acute hazards, though it still differentiates within Austria. In portfolio-readiness terms, the source is only partly ready: once queried via the ThinkHazard! API, it differentiates between Austrian districts but not within a single district.

KryoMon.AT is a publicly funded research consortium coordinated by the University of Graz, involving multiple Austrian universities, the Austrian and Bavarian Academies of Sciences, GeoSphere Austria and several associations (KryoMon.AT, n.d.; ORF Steiermark, 2026). It provides periodic reports on permafrost, glacier and snow trends covering permafrost hazard at station-based granularity across selected Austrian alpine sites (KryoMon.AT, n.d.). The source is accessed through a reports/publications website and PDF downloads, and is free of charge. In the context of Template D 01.01, it is relevant to data point 0050 as a secondary source. For an SNCI, the source is conditionally suitable as the best available current context on Austrian permafrost trends, although its station-based reporting cannot be overlaid with individual portfolio locations and is therefore unsuitable for exposure-level classification. In portfolio-readiness terms, the source is not ready: the information exists only in narrative PDF reports, not as structured per-location data, so no automated pipeline can be built.

This is a public register operated by Statistik Austria (Statistik Austria, n.d.). It provides the official OeNACE 2025 (NACE Rev. 2.1) economic-activity code for each Austrian company, keyed to the Firmenbuch number, covering the full national company register at entity-level granularity (Statistik Austria, n.d.). The source is accessed through direct bulk download in CSV format and is free of charge under a CC BY 4.0 licence, published as a High Value Dataset under Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/138. In the context of Template D 01.01, it is relevant to the NACE subsector dimension as a primary source. For an SNCI, the source is suitable because it is the only identified source that is simultaneously official, freely accessible in bulk and directly joinable to a loan portfolio via the Firmenbuch number, although companies without an assigned OeNACE code, and unregistered sole traders, remain unmatched. In portfolio-readiness terms, the source is fully ready: a direct join on the Firmenbuchnummer assigns the OeNACE code to each exposure with no geocoding or spatial processing needed.

Wirtschafts-Compass is a commercial Austrian company-data service operated by Compass-Verlag GmbH (Compass-Verlag, n.d.). It provides an editorially enriched OeNACE classification per entity, covering the Austrian company landscape at entity-level granularity, delivered with daily currency (Compass-Verlag, n.d.). The source is accessed through an API and a web portal, and is paid, though the operator states that the finance and insurance sector is among its long-standing customers, meaning many Austrian banking-sector institutions may already hold an institutional licence (Compass-Verlag, n.d.-b). In the context of Template D 01.01, it is relevant to the NACE subsector dimension as a secondary source. For an SNCI, the source is conditionally suitable because it complements the HVD dataset operationally where an existing licence makes a single query simpler than a bulk join, although its classification is editorially enriched rather than the official statistical assignment. In portfolio-readiness terms, the source is fully ready on the same basis as HVD: the API returns a differentiating classification directly for each queried entity.

Coverage was originally set uniformly to "partial" across 10 of 12 matrix hazards with identical granularity text, without per-hazard verification. Verified against the EEA's own 32-index / 16-hazard / 6-category index set (EEA, 2021): permafrost, landslide and soil erosion are not represented at all and were corrected to "none"; heat_stress and water_stress are only indirect proxies (UTCI; aridity), not dedicated categories; and the true resolution of the source's own report table is three European macro-regions, not NUTS 1/2 as previously stated.

Originally soil_erosion=full, glacial_lake=partial, heat_stress=partial, water_stress=partial with uniform reasoning. Verified against the JRC's own 2023 technical report (JRC136527, Table 5 "List of hazards addressed currently on the RDH"): only River flood, Coastal flood, Earthquake, Landslide, Forest fire and Subsidence have a modelled Risk Analysis layer. "Subsidence" is a physically distinct process from soil erosion, so soil_erosion corrected to none. glacial_lake, heat_stress and water_stress do not appear in either the Risk Analysis or Loss Data catalogues and were corrected to none. storm, heavy_precip, heat_wave and drought remain partial but are now documented as historical loss-record coverage only (Loss Data module), not modelled hazard layers.

Originally heat_stress=full and wildfire=partial. Verified: CDS hosts the same shared EEA/C3S 32-index dataset as Climate-ADAPT (sis-ecde-climate-indicators), so heat_stress is only the same UTCI proxy noted for Climate-ADAPT and was corrected to partial for consistency. wildfire was corrected to full after confirming a dedicated, purpose-built "Fire danger indices historical data" dataset (CEMS/EFFIS, ERA5-driven, three national fire-danger rating systems) is directly downloadable from the CDS, not merely derivable from raw variables.

Originally landslide=none, heavy_precip=none, drought=partial, wildfire=partial, heat_stress=full. Verified against the ECB's own indicator methodology page, which explicitly lists: "coastal flooding, river flooding, wildfires, landslides, subsidence, windstorms, water stress, droughts and rainfall variation." landslide was missing entirely and corrected to full; drought and wildfire were under-rated and corrected to full; heavy_precip (rainfall variation) corrected from none to partial. heat_stress corrected from full to partial: not named among the ECB's own 9 listed hazards, despite other ECB communications describing "heat and water stress" as a chronic risk category - flagged as a documentation inconsistency pending clarification.

Originally flood, landslide, storm, heat_wave, drought, water_stress and wildfire were all uniformly partial, and soil_erosion was partial. Verified against GFDRR's ThinkHazard! methodology documentation and the World Bank/GFDRR Global Landslide Hazard Map: flood, heat_wave (extreme heat), water_stress (water scarcity, via a dedicated Water Stress Index) and wildfire have commonly-available probabilistic hazard data and were corrected to full; landslide is covered via a dedicated gridded global dataset and corrected to full. soil_erosion, heat_stress and heavy_precip do not appear as distinct categories anywhere in the ThinkHazard!/Risk Data Library ecosystem and were corrected to none. storm remains partial because ThinkHazard!'s "cyclone" hazard model is tropical-cyclone-oriented and its applicability to European extratropical windstorms was not confirmed. drought remains partial as it is only indirectly inferable from the water-scarcity index, not a distinct event-based drought product.

Originally flood and drought were rated partial. Verified against WRI's own 13-indicator Aqueduct 4.0 framework: dedicated "riverine flood risk" (rfr), "coastal flood risk" (cfr) and "drought risk" (drr) indicators exist by name, not merely inferred from water-stress data, and were corrected to full.

Originally storm=full, heat_wave=full, drought=full, wildfire=partial. Verified against Moody's own consistently published hazard list (floods, heat stress, hurricanes and typhoons, sea-level rise, water stress, wildfires): storm was corrected to none because Moody's names "hurricanes and typhoons" specifically - a tropical-cyclone hazard not applicable to landlocked Austria; heat_wave corrected to none because only "heat stress" (a distinct, chronic indicator) is named, not a separate acute heat-wave product; drought corrected to none as it does not appear in any published Moody's hazard list found; wildfire corrected to full as it is consistently and explicitly named.

Originally soil_erosion=partial, glacial_lake=partial, landslide=partial, heavy_precip/heat_wave/heat_stress/drought/water_stress=full, wildfire=partial. Verified against Munich Re's own 15-hazard "Natural Hazards Edition" list (River Flood, Flash Flood, Storm Surge, Tropical Cyclone, Extratropical Storm, Hail, Tornado, Lightning, Earthquake, Volcano, Tsunami, Wildfire, Avalanche, Landslide, Subsidence): landslide and wildfire corrected to full (explicitly named); soil_erosion and glacial_lake corrected to none (not covered, or - for soil_erosion - only the physically distinct "Subsidence" is covered). heavy_precip, heat_wave, heat_stress, drought and water_stress were downgraded from full to partial: these are not named in the Natural Hazards Edition, and the separate "Climate Change Edition" advertises "13 climate hazards" without naming them individually in the materials reviewed, so full coverage could not be confirmed.

Specific pricing for Moody's physical risk/Climate on Demand data is not publicly disclosed; access is quote-based via direct sales contact. Public aggregate spend estimates exist for Moody's software generally (third-party benchmarking, not company-published), but these cover unrelated products (e.g. EDF-X, Orbis) and are not specific to the physical risk data product, so they are not usable as a cost estimate here.

Two distinct access models exist. (1) Location Risk Intelligence On-Demand: a subscription-free, pay-per-location service for single-location lookups (not full portfolios), priced in tiered packages from EUR 160 per location (5-location package, EUR 800 net) down to EUR 100 per location (50-location package, EUR 5,000 net; 48 credits per location lookup), prices exclude VAT (Munich Re, n.d.-c). (2) The portfolio-scale Natural Hazards Edition / Climate Change Edition subscription (Business/Corporate tiers, with API access) remains quote-based and not publicly priced.

Pay-per-query pricing: from EUR 6 (excl. SPARTACUS-v3 is a public gridded climate dataset operated by GeoSphere Austria, the Austrian federal institute for geology, geophysics, climatology and meteorology (GeoSphere Austria, n.d.-a). It provides observed daily, monthly and quarterly temperature, precipitation and sunshine-duration fields at 1km resolution across Austria since 1961, updated daily (GeoSphere Austria, n.d.-a). The source is accessed through a web interface, a coordinate-based REST API and HTTP bulk download, and is free of charge, published under the CC0 1.0 Public Domain Dedication used for most GeoSphere Austria Data Hub datasets (GeoSphere Austria/re3data, n.d.). In the context of Template D 01.01, it is relevant to data point 0050 as a primary source. For an SNCI, the source is suitable because it provides Austria's highest-resolution national gridded observation dataset, finer than Copernicus CDS' ~0.1-0.25 degree grid, with a coordinate-based API enabling direct point queries. In portfolio-readiness terms, the source is ready: once geocoded, an API query per coordinate returns a differentiating, 1km-resolution value, though converting the raw climate variables into a specific heat-wave or heavy-precipitation indicator requires the bank's own threshold definition.

WINFORE is a public gridded drought-index dataset operated by GeoSphere Austria (GeoSphere Austria, n.d.-b). It provides the Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI) at 30-, 90- and 365-day aggregation windows, plus potential evapotranspiration, derived from SPARTACUS temperature and precipitation fields at 1km resolution across Austria, updated daily (GeoSphere Austria, n.d.-b). The source is accessed through a web interface, a coordinate-based REST API and HTTP bulk download, and is free of charge, published under the CC0 1.0 Public Domain Dedication used for most GeoSphere Austria Data Hub datasets (GeoSphere Austria/re3data, n.d.). In the context of Template D 01.01, it is relevant to data point 0050 as a primary source. For an SNCI, the source is suitable because it is a dedicated, purpose-built national drought index at fine resolution, filling a gap not covered by any other Austrian source in this matrix, although the SPEI value is a standardised statistical anomaly rather than an absolute water-deficit measure. In portfolio-readiness terms, the source is ready: once geocoded, an API query per coordinate returns a differentiating, 1km-resolution SPEI value directly.

Spectra is a commercial physical climate risk platform operated by Climate X Ltd, a UK-based company founded in 2020 (Technology Tools, n.d.). It provides asset-level modelled physical hazard scores and financial loss projections across up to 16 hazards (including flooding, storms, tropical cyclones, storm surge, heat stress, wildfires, landslides and subsidence), with scenario projections to 2100 (Repath, n.d.; Net Zero Compare, n.d.). The source is accessed through a commercial SaaS platform and an API, and is paid, subject to a quote-based commercial licence; third-party estimates (not operator-confirmed) suggest a "mid-market" price range of roughly EUR 20,000-60,000 per year for a 30-100 asset portfolio (Repath, n.d.). In the context of Template D 01.01, it is relevant to data points 0050 and 0090–0130 as a primary source. For an SNCI, the source is conditionally suitable because it offers ready-made, high-granularity asset-level scores integrable via API, although its cost and enterprise-SaaS positioning may still exceed a typical SNCI's budget scale. In portfolio-readiness terms, the source is fully ready: the API returns a differentiating, asset-level score directly, with no further spatial processing required.

ClimateScore Global is a commercial physical climate risk platform operated by Jupiter Intelligence, Inc., a US company founded in 2017 (aigreentools.com, n.d.). It provides asset-level modelled physical hazard scores and finance-grade loss metrics across 9 physical perils (including flood, heat, drought, tropical cyclones, wind and wildfire), across 3 emissions scenarios in 5-year increments to 2100, based on peer-reviewed CMIP6/ERA5 science (aigreentools.com, n.d.). The source is accessed through a commercial SaaS platform and an API, and is paid, subject to a quote-based enterprise licence; Jupiter's own CEO has stated subscription pricing ranges from USD 25,000 to multi-million-dollar contracts depending on scope, with full portfolio deployments typically at six-figure annual commitments (Trellis/Clancy, 2022; Repath, n.d.). In the context of Template D 01.01, it is relevant to data points 0050 and 0090–0130 as a primary source. For an SNCI, the source is conditionally suitable because of its extensive, scientifically validated hazard and financial-metric coverage; the lower end of its stated pricing range may be within reach for a well-resourced SNCI for a limited scope, although full portfolio deployments are likely well above a typical SNCI's budget scale. In portfolio-readiness terms, the source is fully ready: the API returns a differentiating, asset-level score directly, with no further spatial processing required.
